title: Why It Breaks in Matches
seoTitle: Why You Play Worse in Matches Than in Practice | Amir Ardekanian
description: Your shot works in drills and fails in tennis matches. Why practice doesn't always travel, what the research says, and how to move a skill into your match.

blocks.text: You hit the ball well in practice. Then the match starts and your best shot goes missing.
It can look like bad luck or nerves. Sometimes it is nerves, and Practise Under Pressure covers that. This article covers the other cause: the shot was learned in conditions a match doesn't give you.

Here's what a drill hides from you and what the research says about it. Then I'll show you how to move a skill from the basket into your matches. It follows on from The Practice Ladder, so read that first if you haven't.
Your drill hid your opponent

In a basket drill the ball arrives with no body behind it. In a match, your opponent's body tells you things before the ball does. Where they'll hit it. How hard. You pick that up without trying, and it's part of how you get ready for the shot.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: Skilled tennis players predict the direction of an opponent's stroke faster than less skilled players, partly because they look in better places. In another study, when players could see the ball in flight, they predicted a serve's direction better with a real return movement than with a spoken answer. The experts' edge was bigger in the real-movement condition.
A basket feed gives you none of that. There's nothing to read, so that part of your game isn't being trained.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: Cricket is the closest test. Teenage batters faced a bowling machine and a real bowler, both at the same speed. Against the machine they started their movement later and moved differently. The researchers warned against leaning on machines in development programmes.
A basket feed is the tennis version of that machine. Nobody has tested it on tennis players. I'd still expect the same.
Your drill was too friendly to prove anything
Drills are kind. The ball comes where you expect, and you always get another go. So the shot looks great, and you feel it's ready.
But how you perform in practice is often a poor guide to what you've learned. A drill shows what works right now, in those conditions. Change the conditions and you find out what you really have.

blocks.label: The research
blocks.text: A review of the learning research found that people often mistake how they perform during practice for what they've learned.
How to make a drill travel

You don't have to throw the baskets away. Drills still work. In a study of ten-year-old girls learning a forehand, one group did repetitive drills and the other played games with changed equipment and rules. Both groups got more accurate.
What you do is change one thing at a time, so the drill gets closer to a match.

blocks.label: Upgrade 1 — The opponent
blocks.text: Serve to a returner, not to an empty box. Hit with a partner who hits back, not with a basket.

blocks.label: Upgrade 2 — The next shot
blocks.text: Serve and then hit one more. Hit your slice, then play the ball that comes back.

blocks.label: Upgrade 3 — A choice
blocks.text: Give yourself two targets and pick one as the ball comes. Better still, let your partner decide where the ball goes.

blocks.label: Upgrade 4 — The score
blocks.text: Play the same pattern as a point and keep score.

Change one thing, then watch what changes. In the junior serve study, the players didn't simply get better or worse. They traded one thing for another. One group went for speed, another for placement. Notice what you give up each time you add a piece.
When it still breaks in a match
A match isn't the place to rebuild a stroke. You have too much else to think about.
Step back down the ladder instead. Find the step where the shot still holds, make it solid there and climb again. Where it breaks tells you what's missing.

items: Holds in drills, breaks in rallies: the live ball is the problem. Work on reading the ball.
Holds in rallies, breaks in points: the decision is the problem. Add a choice.
Holds in points, breaks in practice matches: the stakes are the problem. Add some pressure.

blocks.label: My rule
blocks.text: Judge a drill by what shows up in your next match.
Based on Soderstrom and Bjork (2015), Pinder et al. (2009), Williams et al. (2002), Farrow and Abernethy (2003), Krause et al. (2019) and Lee et al. (2014).
